bills.title: Rural health care; Alabama Health Command established to designate an AI-assisted health platform in rural communities
bills.desc: Alabama's HB 280 would create the Alabama Health Command, an independent agency under a director appointed by the Governor, to designate an Alabama-headquartered business to develop a uniform virtual AI-assisted health platform for rural communities. The platform would give consumers health management services such as education, scheduling and navigation to rural providers, without diagnosis or treatment. Rural providers that contract to use it would be exempt from competitive bid laws. Referred to House Ways and Means General Fund on January 20, 2026; the bill died when the 2026 regular session ended without final passage.

bills.title: Artificial intelligence; regulate use in health coverage decisions
bills.desc: Alabama's HB 515 (2025, as introduced) would have limited how health insurers use AI, algorithms or other software in utilization review. Medical necessity determinations would always have been made by a licensed physician or other competent health care professional. Insurers would have had to disclose AI use to enrollees and contracting providers, periodically review outcomes, and face civil suits for compensatory or punitive damages. Introduced April 3, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Insurance; it died in committee when the 2025 session ended.

bills.title: Health care plans; to regulate the use of artificial intelligence in determinations of coverage
bills.desc: Alabama's SB 63 (Act 2026-589) limits how health benefit plan providers, including insurers, HMOs and utilization review contractors, use AI in prior authorization. AI-assisted medical necessity determinations must rest on the enrollee's medical history, clinical circumstances presented by the requesting provider and other information in the record, and any denial, delay or modification must be made by a licensed physician or other competent health care professional. Providers must certify their AI annually to the Department of Insurance, disclose its use and review its outcomes. Fines up to $5,000 for repeat violations. Signed April 16, 2026; effective October 1, 2026.

bills.title: Rural health care; Alabama Health Command established to designate an AI-assisted health platform in rural communities
bills.desc: Alabama's SB 97 would create the Alabama Health Command, an independent agency under a director appointed by the Governor, to designate an Alabama-headquartered business to develop a uniform virtual AI-assisted health platform for rural communities. The platform would give consumers health management services such as education, scheduling and navigation to rural providers, without diagnosis or treatment. Rural providers that contract to use it would be exempt from competitive bid laws. Referred to Senate Healthcare on January 13, 2026; the bill died when the 2026 regular session ended without final passage.

bills.title: Concerning Artificial Intelligence, Algorithms, And Other Automated Technologies; And To Regulate Certain Practices Of Healthcare Insurers.
bills.desc: Arkansas HB 1297 (2025), as engrossed, would have added a subchapter (Ark. Code §§ 23-63-2101 to 2113) regulating healthcare insurers' use of AI and automated decision-making in utilization review. Insurers would have had to disclose algorithm details from January 1, 2026, give explanations for AI-supported denials, and have a clinician licensed in Arkansas review adverse prior authorization determinations. The Insurance Commissioner could fine up to $25,000 per determination. The author withdrew it on April 1, 2025.

bills.title: To Prohibit Healthcare Providers And Healthcare Insurers From Using Artificial Intelligence In The Delivery Of Healthcare Services Or The Generation …
bills.desc: Arkansas HB 1816 (2025) would have added Ark. Code § 17-80-123 to bar healthcare providers and healthcare insurers from using artificial intelligence in delivering healthcare services or generating medical records, unless the AI is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and verified by a quality assurance laboratory. It was filed March 17, 2025, referred to the House Public Health, Welfare and Labor Committee, and withdrawn by its author on April 14, 2025.

Before a claim or prior-authorization denial based on medical necessity, the insurer's medical director must individually review the denial, use independent medical judgment and not rely solely on recommendations from any other source.

bills.title: Artificial intelligence; nursing tasks; pilot
bills.desc: Arizona's HB 4080 (2026) would have established an artificial intelligence nursing innovation pilot program in the Department of Health Services to develop and test AI that performs nursing-adjacent tasks or workflows in a clinical setting. The department would select not more than five technology vendors recommended by an advisory committee. The bill was assigned to House Rules, held there, and died when the 2026 session ended June 13, 2026.

bills.title: Health care services: artificial intelligence.
bills.desc: California's AB 1979 sets rules for AI in clinical care. Health facilities such as hospitals, clinics, physician offices and group practices must take reasonable steps so licensed providers keep independent professional judgment whenever care is informed by a clinical decision support system, and may not use AI to independently perform licensed clinical work, or to direct unlicensed staff doing it. Businesses offering health care chatbots that consumers use to manage their health information or to diagnose, treat or manage a condition are treated as health care providers under the state's medical privacy law (CMIA). Signed September 30, 2026 (Chapter 854); effective January 1, 2027.

bills.title: Health care services: artificial intelligence.
bills.desc: Vetoed. AB 2575 would have barred California employers from retaliating against workers providing direct patient care based solely on their override of, or reliance on, a clinical decision support system (AI that aids decisions on timing of care, diagnosis or treatment), with enforcement by the Labor Commissioner. In lawsuits over harm from such a system, its developer or deployer could not have argued that a clinician's failure to override it cut off liability. Governor Newsom vetoed it on September 30, 2026, saying its anti-retaliation test set a higher bar than other protections and would make the Labor Commissioner judge the medical standard of care.

bills.title: Health care services: artificial intelligence.
bills.desc: California requires hospitals and other health facilities, clinics, physician offices and group practices that use generative AI to write or speak patient communications about clinical information to include a disclaimer that the message was AI-generated and clear instructions for reaching a human health care provider or other appropriate person. The disclaimer goes at the top of letters and emails, stays on screen in chats and video, and is spoken at the start and end of audio. Messages a licensed provider reads and reviews are exempt, as are administrative messages like scheduling and billing. Effective January 1, 2025.

Health plans and disability insurers that use AI for utilization review must base decisions on the enrollee's individual clinical history; a medical-necessity denial must be made by a licensed physician or other licensed health care professional.

bills.title: Advertisement claims: health-related consumer products and services: digital replicas and synthetic performers.
bills.desc: California's SB 1146 (Gonzalez) would add Business and Professions Code 651.4, requiring a person who creates an advertisement for a health-related consumer product or service that includes a digital replica or synthetic performer depicted as a health care provider to include a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the provider was AI-generated or altered or that no human provider is depicted. Passed the Senate 36-0 on May 18, 2026; held in Assembly Appropriations August 13, 2026; it did not pass.

bills.title: Health care services: artificial intelligence.
bills.desc: California's SB 503 targets bias in clinical AI. Developers and deployers (health facilities, clinics and medical practices) of clinical decision support systems, AI that aids decisions on timing of care, diagnosis or treatment, must make reasonable efforts to find systems with known or foreseeable risk of biased impacts based on protected characteristics. Developers must mitigate those risks and give deployers a statement of uses and risks plus documentation on training data, bias testing and monitoring; deployers must monitor the systems and take reasonable steps to mitigate bias. Signed September 30, 2026 (Chapter 857); effective January 1, 2027.

bills.title: Mental health and artificial intelligence working group.
bills.desc: California's SB 579 (as amended in the Senate March 26, 2025) would require the Secretary of Government Operations to appoint, on or before July 1, 2026, a mental health and artificial intelligence working group to evaluate AI's role in mental health settings. The group would hold at least three public meetings, report to the Legislature by July 1, 2028 and issue a followup report by January 1, 2030, and the provisions would be repealed January 1, 2031. It was held in the Senate Appropriations Committee on May 23, 2025 and is listed as an inactive bill that died.

bills.title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Health Care
bills.desc: Colorado's HB 26-1139 regulates AI in utilization review. Insurers, PBMs, utilization review organizations, behavioral health administrative services organizations and managed care entities that use it must ensure the AI relies on the individual's clinical information, not solely group data, does not unlawfully discriminate, keeps audit logs and is periodically reviewed, and must disclose their AI use and human oversight to regulators. A medical-necessity denial may not rest solely on AI output without a competent clinician's review and approval. Health plans, Medicaid and CHP+ may not pay for psychotherapy conducted by AI. Signed June 2, 2026 (Chapter 325); effective January 1, 2027.
Prohibits AI therapy chatbots; limits AI use by licensed psychotherapy providers.

bills.title: Automated Decision-Making Technology
bills.desc: Colorado's SB 26-189 repeals and reenacts the 2024 AI Act as rules for automated decision-making technology (ADMT) that materially influences consequential decisions such as hiring, lending, housing and health care. Developers must document covered ADMT for deployers; deployers must give notice before use, explain adverse outcomes within 30 days and, on request, give correction steps and, where commercially reasonable, human review. Signed May 14, 2026 (Chapter 131); applies from January 1, 2027. A stipulated April 27, 2026 order in X. AI LLC v. Weiser bars AG enforcement of 2026 laws replacing SB 24-205 for violations through 14 days after a ruling on xAI's planned injunction motion.

bills.title: Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act
bills.desc: Colorado's SB 24-205 (the Colorado AI Act) covers high-risk AI that makes, or is a substantial factor in making, consequential decisions such as hiring, lending, housing, insurance and health care. Developers and deployers must use reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination; deployers need risk programs, impact assessments and notices. Signed May 17, 2024 (Chapter 198). Duties run from June 30, 2026 (SB 25B-004) until SB 26-189 replaces Part 17 on January 1, 2027. Under a stipulated April 27, 2026 order in X. AI LLC v. Weiser (D. Colo.), the Attorney General may not start enforcement over violations through 14 days after a ruling on xAI's planned preliminary-injunction motion.

bills.title: An Act Prohibiting Health Insurers From Using Artificial Intelligence As The Primary Method To Deny Health Insurance Claims.
bills.desc: Connecticut's HB 5587 (Rep. Menapace) is a proposed bill that would amend the general statutes to prohibit any health insurer from using artificial intelligence as the primary method to deny health insurance claims. The text is a one-sentence statement of purpose with no definitions, penalties or procedures. Referred to the Joint Committee on Insurance and Real Estate January 21, 2025; it did not advance and died when the 2025 session ended.

bills.title: An Act Prohibiting Health Insurers From Using Artificial Intelligence To Deny Health Insurance Claims.
bills.desc: Connecticut's HB 5590 (2025) was a short proposed bill with no operative text, stating its intent to amend the general statutes to prohibit any health insurer from using artificial intelligence to deny health insurance claims. It was referred to the Insurance and Real Estate Committee on January 21, 2025 and died when the 2025 session ended.

bills.title: An Act Prohibiting Health Carriers From Using Artificial Intelligence In The Evaluation And Determination Of Patient Care.
bills.desc: Connecticut's SB 447 (2025) was a short proposed bill with no operative text, stating its intent to amend title 38a of the general statutes to prohibit health carriers from using artificial intelligence in the evaluation and determination of patient care, to safeguard patient access to testing, medications and procedures. It was referred to the Insurance and Real Estate Committee on January 10, 2025 and died when the 2025 session ended.

bills.title: An Act Prohibiting Health Insurers From Using Software Tools To Automatically Downcode Health Insurance Claims.
bills.desc: Connecticut's Proposed SB 817 (2025), introduced by Sen. Looney, would have amended title 38a of the general statutes to prohibit any health insurer from using a software tool, including artificial intelligence or an algorithm, to automatically downcode or deny a health insurance claim submitted by a health care provider without detailed review by a clinical peer. The filed text is a brief proposed bill with a statement of purpose. Referred to the Joint Committee on Insurance and Real Estate January 21, 2025; it died when the 2025 session ended.

bills.title: Private Review Agents; certain decisions with regard to the provision of insurance coverage for healthcare services shall not be based solely on arti…
bills.desc: Georgia Act 411, effective January 1, 2027, adds O.C.G.A. 33-46-7.1 for health insurance utilization review. Private review agents and utilization review entities may use AI and other software tools as part of a utilization review plan that meets state standards and Insurance Commissioner rules, including to automate tasks and take part in decisions. But no adverse determination may be issued to a patient until a natural person qualified as a private review agent or utilization review entity conducts a review in which a clinical peer participates, and AI may never supersede that clinical peer's judgment.

bills.title: Relating To Health Care.
bills.desc: Hawaii's House Bill 1787 (2026) would have set rules for health carriers and utilization review organizations that use AI, algorithms or other software tools in utilization review: determinations would have to rest on individual clinical history, be open to commissioner inspection and be reviewed at least quarterly. It would also have barred using these tools to deny, delay or modify care, and required a licensed provider to review adverse actions. It was referred to committees January 26, 2026 and not enacted.

bills.title: Relating To The Patients' Bill Of Rights.
bills.desc: Hawaii's HB 2537 (2026), the Patients' Bill of Rights, would have amended HRS chapter 432E for managed care plans. It would set prior authorization deadlines (one business day urgent, three non-urgent), require notice and independent board-certified clinician review before an adverse action to which an automated decision support tool materially contributed, and require governance and bias-testing records by June 30, 2027. It was referred to HLT and CPC February 2, 2026 and died.

bills.title: Relating To The Hawaii Patients' Bill Of Rights And Responsibilities Act.
bills.desc: Hawaii's SB 2167 (2026) would have amended HRS chapter 432E, the Patients' Bill of Rights, to set prior authorization deadlines (one business day urgent, three non-urgent) and require that a denial initiated by an automated decision system be reviewed and co-signed by a board-certified specialist, with written notice to enrollees and providers whenever such a system is used. It was referred to HHS and CPN January 26, 2026 and died.

bills.title: Relating To Artificial Intelligence.
bills.desc: Hawaii's SB 2585 (2026) would have required the Department of Health, with other agencies, to establish an AI-enhanced online clearinghouse of evidence-based treatment and prevention programs, use AI to classify programs by evidence level and cultural responsiveness, and have any AI model regularly audited for transparency, fairness and bias mitigation. The appropriation amount was blank. It was referred to committees January 28, 2026 and died.

bills.title: Relating To Health Care.
bills.desc: Hawaii's SB 2768 (2026) would have barred health carriers and utilization review organizations from using AI, algorithms or software tools to deny, delay or modify a determination to provide health care services, and would have required a licensed health care provider to independently review any adverse action before a carrier issues it. It was referred to HHS/LBT and CPN on January 30, 2026 and was not enacted.

bills.title: Relating To The Patients' Bill Of Rights.
bills.desc: Hawaii's Senate Bill 3027 (2026), which calls itself the Hawaii Patients' Bill of Rights of 2025, would have set prior authorization deadlines for health carriers (one business day urgent, three non-urgent) and required written disclosure of any automated decision support tool used in utilization review. A board-certified clinician would have had to independently approve any adverse action the tool materially contributed to. It was referred to committee January 30, 2026 and not enacted. It would have taken effect July 1, 2026.

bills.title: A bill for an act relating to the requirements for chatbot deployers, including required protocols, limitations on data collection, and requirements …
bills.desc: Not law. HF 2204 would have required anyone offering a chatbot to the public in Iowa to keep protocols to detect, respond to and reduce harm to users, putting user safety first, and to collect only the data it needs. Deployers would have had to use age verification to keep minors from AI companions (chatbots that simulate a romantic or emotional bond), get permission before offering chatbots that impersonate real people, and meet strict conditions, including a licensed professional's recommendation and clinical trial evidence, before offering therapeutic chatbots to minors. It was referred to committee on January 29, 2026 and died when the 2026 session adjourned.

bills.title: A bill for an act relating to health carriers standards of conduct; utilization review organizations, artificial intelligence, audits, and prior auth…
bills.desc: Iowa's HF 2635 is a health insurance and certificate-of-need law. Its AI rule (Iowa Code § 514F.8(2A)) lets a utilization review organization use an AI-based algorithm or system for the initial review of a prior authorization request, but for a request based on medical necessity AI may not be the sole basis for denying, delaying or downgrading it. The act also requires denials to be made by a same- or similar-specialty physician or clinical peer, sets audit deadlines, bars prior authorization for certain cancer screenings and inpatient emergencies, and raises certificate-of-need thresholds. Signed May 13, 2026 (Acts Chapter 1087); effective July 1, 2026, with many rules applying from 2027.

bills.title: A bill for an act relating to chatbots, including deployer requirements and interactions with minors.(Formerly HSB 647.)
bills.desc: Iowa's HF 2715 (formerly HSB 647) would require deployers of AI companions, public-facing chatbots and therapeutic chatbots to keep harm-response and self-harm protocols, disclose at the start and every three hours that the user is talking to AI, and take extra steps for minors. The attorney general could seek civil penalties up to $2,500 per violation. On the House calendar since February 24, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: A bill for an act relating to the licensure of artificial intelligence augmented and autonomous service providers, and including penalties.
bills.desc: Iowa's HSB 766, a House Appropriations study bill, would create a board of autonomous medical practice to license AI augmented and autonomous service providers (AAASPs) that run clinical AI services. A license would be required for fully autonomous AI and for certain advisory and supervised AI. Providers would face patient disclosures, a duty of loyalty, insurance and bond requirements, and civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation per day. A subcommittee recommended passage March 24, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: A bill for an act relating to utilization review organizations' use of artificial intelligence, prior authorization determinations and exemptions, an…
bills.desc: Iowa's SF 2421 (formerly SSB 3118) would have let utilization review organizations use an AI-based algorithm for initial review of prior authorization requests but not as the sole basis to deny, delay or downgrade a medical-necessity request, and would have required review by a qualified reviewer or clinical peer, written reasons, and deadlines for claim audits. HF 2635 was substituted and SF 2421 was withdrawn March 4, 2026.

bills.title: A bill for an act relating to utilization review organizations, prior authorizations and exemptions, medical billing, and independent review organizations.
bills.desc: The bill addresses utilization review organizations, prior authorizations, and medical billing practices in Iowa.

bills.title: INS-ADVERSE DETERMINATION
bills.desc: Illinois' Public Act 103-0656 (HB 2472) is a broad health insurance act (explanation-of-benefits statements, prior authorization penalties, utilization review accreditation, adverse determinations). Its AI-related part covers algorithmic automated processes in utilization review: even when a plan or utilization review program uses one, only a clinical peer may make an adverse medical necessity determination or review an appeal. Programs using such processes must use objective, evidence-based criteria compliant with URAC or NCQA standards, set by board-certified physicians, and file proof with their registration. Approved July 19, 2024; effective January 1, 2025.

bills.title: Registered Nurse Use of AI
bills.desc: Illinois's HB 4804 (104th General Assembly) would amend the Nurse Practice Act to set rules for registered nurses' use of AI, including a bar on substituting AI for nursing services, patient notice and confidentiality protections, and discipline for violations. Health care entities deploying AI in direct patient care would have to keep validation and bias monitoring records. Re-referred to Rules Committee on March 27, 2026.

bills.title: IDPH-DIAGNOSTIC ALGORITHM
bills.desc: Illinois's HB 5115 (103rd General Assembly) would have amended the University of Illinois Hospital Act, the Hospital Licensing Act and the Medical Patient Rights Act. Before using a diagnostic algorithm to diagnose a patient, a hospital would have to confirm it is certified by the Departments of Public Health and Innovation and Technology, is as or more accurate than other means, and is not the only diagnosis method available. It was not passed before the 103rd General Assembly ended (Session Sine Die, January 7, 2025).

bills.title: NETWORK ADEQUACY-STANDARDS
bills.desc: The Health Care Protection Act is a broad health insurance reform covering network adequacy, prior authorization, step therapy and short-term plans. Its automated decision provision amends Section 85 of the Managed Care Reform and Patient Rights Act (215 ILCS 134/85) on utilization review programs. Only a clinical peer may make adverse medical necessity determinations. A health care professional, an accredited algorithmic automated process, or both together may certify (approve) medical necessity in line with accreditation standards, and an automated process may be used to refer a case to a clinical peer for a possible denial. Effective January 1, 2025.

bills.title: DFPR-AI-MENTAL HEALTH SERVICE
bills.desc: Illinois's HB 5649 (103rd General Assembly) would have made it an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud Act for a licensed mental health professional to provide mental health services through AI without first obtaining the patient's informed consent and disclosing the use of AI tools, with matching grounds for discipline in the professional licensing Acts. It was not passed before the 103rd General Assembly ended (Session Sine Die, January 7, 2025).
Prohibits payor from using automated process to downcode a claim bypassing billing info; downcoding must be made or reviewed by a natural person.

bills.title: REGISTERED NURSE USE OF AI
bills.desc: Illinois's SB 3702 would amend the Nurse Practice Act to bar AI systems from providing nursing services in place of a registered professional nurse in direct patient care, require a nurse to get patient consent before AI records or analyzes an encounter, and require written notice that AI supports but does not replace the nurse. Health care entities employing nurses and deploying AI in direct patient care would have to keep validation and bias monitoring records, train nurses, and not rely solely on AI for staffing, triage, admission, discharge or transfer decisions. Introduced February 5, 2026; re-referred to Assignments May 22, 2026 under Senate Rule 3-9(a); it has not passed either house.

bills.title: Various mental health and insurance matters.
bills.desc: Indiana's HB 1201 (2026) would have barred using an AI system to impersonate or substitute for a licensed mental health professional in interactions that must be performed by one (discipline under IC 25-1-9; a board could impose a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation). It also covered insurance: downcoding limits, mental health reimbursement parity with medical providers relative to Medicare, a 180-day audit and recoupment window, and out-of-network balance-billing limits. Referred to the Insurance Committee January 5, 2026; it was not passed before the 2026 session ended.
Insurers may not use AI as the sole basis to downcode a claim without human review of the medical record, and must disclose AI use in prior-authorization adverse determinations and downcoding.

bills.title: Disclosure of artificial intelligence use in health care.
bills.desc: Indiana's HB 1620 would have required a health care provider that uses AI technology to make or inform any decision in a patient's care, or to generate any part of a communication to the patient (including through a chat bot), to disclose that use to the patient. An insurer providing accident and sickness coverage would have had the same duty toward an insured. Introduced January 21, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Public Health; the Indiana General Assembly's record marks it dead.

bills.title: Enacting the use of artificial intelligence in medical decisions transparency act and requiring that all medical necessity determinations be made by …
bills.desc: Kansas's SB 467 (2026) would have enacted the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Medical Decisions Transparency Act. Health insurers and utilization review organizations using AI, algorithms or software tools for utilization review would have had to ensure the tool bases decisions on the enrollee's clinical information and does not supplant provider decision-making, and the tool could not deny, delay or modify care on medical necessity; only a licensed physician or competent licensed professional could. Referred to committee February 4, 2026; Died in Committee April 10, 2026.

bills.title: AN ACT relating to mental health chatbots.
bills.desc: Kentucky's HB 641 (the Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Act, as introduced) would add sections to KRS Chapter 367 regulating suppliers of mental health chatbots, AI systems that use generative AI to hold therapy-like conversations. Suppliers could not sell or share users' health information or input, would have to label and disclose any advertising, and would have to disclose every 30 minutes that the chatbot is AI. The Attorney General could fine up to $2,500 per violation. Introduced February 13, 2026 and referred to the House Small Business & Information Technology Committee; it died in committee when the session ended.
Licensed professionals must verbally disclose use of recording/transcription software before recording an appointment for AI transcription.

bills.title: Establishes requirements for health insurance issuers using artificial intelligence or automated decision systems. (8/1/26)
bills.desc: Louisiana's SB246 would have set rules for health insurers, pharmacy benefit managers and independent review organizations that use AI or automated decision systems in utilization review: no use that denies, delays or modifies care, adverse determinations signed by a physician who reviewed the record, disclosure of AI use, and a presumption that AI-influenced adverse decisions are invalid on appeal. The Senate withdrew it from its files May 28, 2026, so it died.

bills.title: Provides for the regulation of mental health chatbots that use artificial intelligence technology. (gov sig)
bills.desc: Louisiana's SB5 would have required operators of AI mental health chatbots to disclose clearly that the chatbot is AI and not a human, to maintain protocols for suicidal ideation, self-harm and harm to others, and not to sell or share users' identifiable health information. It would also have restricted advertising in chatbot conversations. The Attorney General could seek fines up to $10,000 per violation after a 45-day cure notice. It stayed in Senate Health and Welfare and died.

bills.title: Relative to AI health communications and informed patient consent
bills.desc: Massachusetts' H 1210 would give patients the right to be told when health information they get was generated by AI, with instructions for reaching a human provider if the provider had not reviewed it. Health insurance carriers would have to disclose AI or automated decision tools used in claims review and file an annual report on AI algorithms and training data used in utilization review, with a bias attestation. Referred to Financial Services February 27, 2025; on February 9, 2026 it accompanied a study order (H 5066) and did not advance as its own bill.

bills.title: Relative to the use of artificial intelligence and other software tools in healthcare decision-making
bills.desc: Massachusetts S2632 would bar AI from denying, delaying or modifying health care on medical-necessity grounds, requiring a licensed professional to decide, and would limit AI in therapy: licensed therapists may use it only for administrative or supplementary support, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation. Committee recommended ought to pass and referred to Senate Ways and Means April 2, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Relative to the use of artificial intelligence and other software tools in healthcare decision-making
bills.desc: Massachusetts S46 would amend G.L. c. 176O, s. 12 so that insurers using AI, algorithms or software for medical-necessity review may not let the tool deny, delay or modify care; only a licensed physician or competent licensed professional may decide. On October 16, 2025 it accompanied new draft S2632, which on April 2, 2026 was sent to Senate Ways and Means with an ought-to-pass recommendation.

bills.title: Health Insurance - Use of Artificial Intelligence - Human Evaluation
bills.desc: Maryland's HB 1385 (2026, first reader text) would have amended Insurance section 15-10B-05.1 so that audits and compliance reviews of AI, algorithms or software tools used by carriers for utilization review include a human evaluation of the patient's medical records by a licensed health care professional who can question, modify or override the tool's determination, and quarterly performance reviews include a human evaluation of real-world health outcomes. It had a House Health hearing set for March 12, 2026 and died when the 2026 session ended.

bills.title: Health Insurance - Artificial Intelligence, Adverse Decisions, and Grievances - Reporting Requirements
bills.desc: Maryland's HB 697 (2025) would have required each health insurance carrier to report quarterly to the Insurance Commissioner on how it creates, deploys and uses artificial intelligence or automated decision-making systems (new Insurance section 15-147), and expanded the demographic and call-center data carriers report on grievances and adverse decisions (section 15-10A-06). The sponsor withdrew it on February 17, 2025, after a canceled February 13 hearing.

Carriers, PBMs and private review agents using AI in utilization review must base decisions on individual clinical history, with the final decision by a physician; quarterly adverse-decision reports must state whether AI was used.

bills.title: An Act to Prohibit the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Denial of Health Insurance Claims
bills.desc: Not law. Maine's LD 1301 would have set conditions, beginning January 1, 2026, on health insurance carriers and their contractors that use artificial intelligence in medical or utilization review decisions to approve, deny, delay or modify coverage. Despite its title, it did not ban AI. AI determinations would have had to rest on the enrollee's medical history and clinical circumstances and not supplant provider decision-making, and could not discriminate. Any denial, delay or modification based on medical necessity would have needed a clinical peer. The committee voted Ought Not To Pass on January 14, 2026; final disposition January 27, 2026.
Prohibits AI therapy/psychotherapy without a licensed professional; unfair trade practice.

bills.title: Insurance: health insurers; use of artificial intelligence tools to make decisions regarding claims; prohibit. Amends 1956 PA 218 (MCL 500.100 - 500.…
bills.desc: Michigan's HB 4536 would add section 3406ss to the Insurance Code of 1956 providing that an insurer that delivers, issues for delivery, or renews in Michigan a health insurance policy shall not deny, modify, or delay a claim based on a review using artificial intelligence. Introduced June 3, 2025; re-referred to the House Committee on Communications and Technology March 19, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Human services: medical services; use of artificial intelligence tools to make decisions regarding claims; prohibit. Amends 1939 PA 280 (MCL 400.1 - …
bills.desc: Michigan's HB 4537 would add section 107b to the social welfare act (1939 PA 280) providing that the department or a contracted health plan shall not deny, modify, or delay a claim under the medical assistance program based on a review using artificial intelligence. Introduced June 3, 2025; re-referred to the House Committee on Communications and Technology March 19, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Algorithm and AI use prohibited during health insurance prior authorization request review.
bills.desc: Minnesota's HF 2500 would have barred a health carrier from using an algorithm or artificial intelligence program when deciding whether to approve or deny a prior authorization request. It would have applied to health plans offered, sold, issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2026. Introduced March 17, 2025 and referred to Commerce Finance and Policy and it never left committee.

bills.title: Commerce policy bill (Laws 2026, chapter 124), including article 3, section 6 barring utilization review organizations from using artificial intellig…
bills.desc: Minnesota's 2026 commerce omnibus (Laws 2026, chapter 124) adds an AI rule to the state's utilization review law. Article 3, section 6 amends Minn. Stat. 62M.09, subd. 3 to prohibit a utilization review organization from exclusively using artificial intelligence to make an adverse determination on coverage of benefits; a clinician must review the denial. AI may still be used in other parts of the review process. Article 1, section 61 also routes civil penalties under the 2026 nudification ban to the victims of crime account. The rest of the act is not AI-related.

bills.title: Prior authorization usage of algorithms or artificial intelligence prohibition provision
bills.desc: Minnesota's SF 3984 would have barred a health carrier from using an algorithm or artificial intelligence program when deciding whether to approve or deny a prior authorization request. It would have applied to health plans offered, sold, issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2026. Introduced February 26, 2026 and referred to Commerce and Consumer Protection and it never left committee.

bills.title: Modifies provisions relating to medical malpractice for the use of artificial intelligence by health care providers
bills.desc: Missouri's SB 1598 would provide that a medical malpractice claim includes a health care provider's negligent use, selection or implementation of artificial intelligence, or undue, detrimental or erroneous reliance on it, in diagnosing, treating and caring for a patient when that negligence or reliance directly causes or contributes to the injury. Such an action would have to be brought within two years of when the negligence or reliance was or should have been discovered. Referred to the Senate General Laws Committee February 5, 2026; the bill died when the 2026 regular session ended in May 2026 without being truly agreed to and finally passed.

bills.title: Mississippi Medical Judgement Protection Act; create.
bills.desc: Mississippi's HB 1717 (2026), the Mississippi Medical Judgment Protection Act, would require a provider or facility whose clinical AI materially contributes to a diagnosis, treatment plan, order or clinical note to disclose that in the medical record and have a licensed clinician accept or reject it. It would bar payers from issuing automated denials or delays of coverage or payment, and require adverse determinations to be reviewed and signed by a physician. It died in committee on February 3, 2026.

bills.title: AI Chatbots-Licensing, Safety, and Privacy.
bills.desc: SB 963 would require a state license from the North Carolina Department of Justice to operate or distribute any chatbot dealing substantially with health information, with evidence of effectiveness, insurance, encryption, fast breach reporting and annual audits. A Chatbot Safety and Privacy Act would give larger chatbot providers a duty of loyalty: respond to users at risk of harm, prevent emotional dependence, disclose at each new interaction that the chatbot is not human and get consent, deidentify data, and keep sensitive data out of training. Users could sue for $1,000 per violation. Pending in the Senate.

AI output may not be the sole basis for denying, delaying or modifying health care services on medical-necessity grounds; AI use in utilization review must be disclosed, including to network providers and enrollees.

bills.title: Relative to health carrier recordkeeping requirements in utilization review, including specifications regarding the use of artificial intelligence.
bills.desc: New Hampshire's HB 1406 (2026), as amended by the House, would require health carriers to keep written records on their use of algorithms and AI in utilization review and require adverse determinations, including payment reductions and down coding, to be made by a qualified health care provider, with written notice and records. It passed the House with amendment on March 11, 2026; the Senate voted it Inexpedient to Legislate on May 7, 2026 and it was killed.

bills.title: Requires collection of data by health insurers regarding health insurance claims and decisions made using automated utilization management systems.
bills.desc: New Jersey's S1029 would require health insurers (payers) to keep and report data on claims, including denials, appeals and prior-authorization outcomes, and would make them disclose whether they use an automated utilization management system (a system that may use AI to recommend or decide coverage) and how many claims it reviewed. A payer determined to have denied at least 20 percent of a year's claims without proper justification would have to repay covered persons for the denied services. Referred to the Senate Commerce Committee January 13, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Revises provisions relating to health insurance. (BDR 57-238)
bills.desc: Nevada's AB 295 (2025) would have set prior authorization deadlines for health carriers (5 days non-urgent, 48 hours urgent, replacing 20 days) and required carriers using AI or automated decision tools for prior authorization to notify insureds in writing, and barred using AI to make adverse determinations or reduce or modify approved care unless a physician (or dentist) independently reviews the request. Carriers would report annually. Under Joint Standing Rule 14.3.1 no further action was allowed after April 12, 2025, so it died.

bills.title: Relates to the use of artificial intelligence by insurers and clinical peer reviewers for utilization review; establishes additional notice requireme…
bills.desc: New York's A 11048 would add Insurance Law § 338 on AI-based algorithms in utilization review. Insurers would have to notify insureds, enrollees and providers of AI use, submit their algorithms and training data to the Superintendent with a certification, and could not use AI as the sole basis to deny, delay or modify care. Fines of up to $5,000 per violation ($10,000 if willful) would apply. Introduced April 24, 2026 and referred to the Insurance Committee; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Provides for notice requirements where an insurer authorized to write accident and health insurance in this state, a corporation organized pursuant t…
bills.desc: New York's A 1456 would add Insurance Law § 338 requiring accident and health insurers, Article 43 corporations and Article 44 HMOs to tell insureds on their public websites about their use or lack of use of AI-based algorithms in utilization review, to submit those algorithms and training data to the Department for certification that bias risk is minimized, and to have clinical peer reviewers document review of individual records before an adverse determination. Fines would be up to $5,000 per violation or $10,000 per willful violation. Referred to Insurance January 7, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Establishes requirements for the use of artificial intelligence, algorithm, or other software tools in utilization review and management; defines art…
bills.desc: New York's A 3991 would add Insurance Law § 3224-e and define artificial intelligence in Insurance Law § 107(a). A health care service plan using an AI, algorithm or other software tool for utilization review or management would have to ensure it bases determinations on the enrollee's history and clinical circumstances, does not supplant provider decision making, does not discriminate, and is open to inspection. Medical necessity denials, delays or modifications would have to be made by a licensed physician or other competent provider. Would take effect immediately. Referred to Insurance January 30, 2025 and January 7, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Prohibits discrimination through the use of clinical algorithms; provides exceptions for clinical algorithms that rely on variables to appropriately …
bills.desc: New York's A 3993 would add Insurance Law § 3243-a providing that an insurer subject to the article shall not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability through the use of clinical algorithms in its decision-making, while permitting clinical algorithms that rely on variables to appropriately make decisions, including to identify, evaluate and address health disparities. Would take effect immediately. Referred to Insurance January 30, 2025 and January 7, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Prescribes requirements and safeguards for the use of an artificial intelligence, algorithm, or other software tool for the purpose of utilization re…
bills.desc: New York's A 8556 would add Public Health Law § 4905-a and Insurance Law § 4905-a. A utilization review agent or disability insurer using AI, an algorithm or another software tool for utilization review based on medical necessity would have to base determinations on the enrollee's clinical history, not solely a group dataset, and the tool could not "deny, delay, or modify health care services" on medical necessity; only a licensed health care professional could. Would take effect on the ninetieth day after it becomes law. Referred to the Insurance Committee May 20, 2025 (and January 7, 2026); it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Provides for notice requirements where an insurer authorized to write accident and health insurance in this state, a corporation organized pursuant t…
bills.desc: New York's A 9149 (2023-2024 session) would have added Insurance Law § 338. Accident and health insurers, article 43 corporations and certified HMOs would have had to post on their websites whether they use AI-based algorithms in utilization review, submit the algorithms and training data to the Department for bias certification, and ensure a clinical peer reviewer documents review of individual clinical records before an adverse determination. Penalties included fines up to $5,000 per violation ($10,000 if willful) and license action. Introduced February 8, 2024 and referred to the Insurance Committee; it never advanced and died at the end of the 2023-2024 session.

bills.title: Requires experts in professional fields to be consulted when developing and maintaining artificial intelligence technology for use in such fields.
bills.desc: New York's A 9219 would add General Business Law §§ 1710 to 1715. A developer of AI intended for a professional domain regulated under Title Eight of the Education Law would have to show that a licensed professional domain expert with three or more years of experience was directly and substantially involved in design, data and training, validation and ongoing risk assessment, and submit documentation to the Attorney General. Penalties up to $50,000 per violation. Would take effect one year after it becomes law. Referred to Science and Technology November 3, 2025 (and January 7, 2026); it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Relates to the use of artificial intelligence by insurers and clinical peer reviewers for utilization review; establishes additional notice requireme…
bills.desc: New York's S 10241 (same as A 11048) would add Insurance Law § 338 and amend the Insurance and Public Health Laws to regulate insurers' use of AI-based algorithms in utilization review. Insurers would give written notice of AI use, submit the algorithms and training data to the superintendent, and could not base a denial, delay or modification of care solely on an algorithm; and, where AI is used, adverse determinations would come only from clinical peer reviewers. Referred to the Senate Insurance Committee May 8, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Prescribes requirements and safeguards for the use of an artificial intelligence, algorithm, or other software tool for the purpose of utilization re…
bills.desc: New York's S 7896 would add Public Health Law § 4905-a and Insurance Law § 4905-a. A utilization review agent using AI, an algorithm or another software tool based on medical necessity must base determinations on the enrollee's clinical history, may not rely solely on a group dataset, and must not let the tool supplant provider decision-making. The tool could not deny, delay or modify services on medical necessity grounds; only a licensed physician or health professional could. Referred to Health January 7, 2026; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Regulate the use of artificial intelligence by health insurers
bills.desc: Ohio's HB 579, the House companion to SB 164 with identical text, would add section 3902.80 requiring health plan issuers to report annually to the superintendent of insurance on their use of AI-based algorithms in utilization review, and barring decisions about a covered person's care based solely on AI results. Medical necessity determinations would require a licensed physician or qualified provider. Introduced November 5, 2025; referred to the House Insurance Committee November 12, 2025.

bills.title: Regulate the use of artificial intelligence by health insurers
bills.desc: Ohio's SB 164 would add section 3902.80 requiring health plan issuers to report annually to the superintendent of insurance on their use of AI-based algorithms in utilization review, and barring decisions about a covered person's care, including denials, delays or modifications based on medical necessity, based solely on AI results. Medical necessity determinations would require a licensed physician or qualified provider. It was introduced April 1, 2025 and referred to the Senate Financial Institutions, Insurance and Technology Committee April 2, 2025.

bills.title: Health insurance; review agents; artificial intelligence system; adverse determinations; effective date.
bills.desc: Oklahoma's HB 3675 (2026), as introduced, would have required a qualified human professional to review any adverse determination made by an algorithm, AI system or automated decision system in utilization review before it is finalized, let the Insurance Commissioner audit use of such systems, and required adverse-determination notices to give reasons and appeal rights. It was referred to the Rules Committee February 11, 2026 and died when the session ended May 14, 2026.

bills.title: Hospital and Medical Services Utilization Review Act; requiring utilization review organization that uses AI to adhere to requirements; prohibiting A…
bills.desc: Oklahoma's SB 1967 (2026), as introduced, would have amended the Hospital and Medical Services Utilization Review Act to set conditions on AI tools used in utilization review by review organizations and insurers, including that the tool not supplant provider decision-making; per the official bill summary, the tool could not deny a claim based on medical necessity. It was referred to a Senate committee February 3, 2026 and died when the session ended May 14, 2026.

bills.title: Relating to downcoding.
bills.desc: Not law. Oregon HB 4054 (2026) would have required health insurers that provide utilization review to tell a provider in writing, within two business days after payment, when AI, an algorithm or other software automatically downcoded a claim, giving the reason and appeal rights, and would have given providers a timely appeal. It had a public hearing in the Information Management and Technology committee and was in committee upon adjournment March 6, 2026.

bills.title: Providing for artificial intelligence in facilities, for artificial intelligence use by insurers and for artificial intelligence use by MA or CHIP ma…
bills.desc: Pennsylvania's HB 1925 (2025-26), as amended (Printer's No. 3963), would add rules for AI in health care facilities, AI use by insurers and AI use by MA or CHIP managed care plans, with duties for the departments of Health, Insurance and Human Services and penalties. The captured text covers the facilities chapter: patient disclosure and responsible-use rules for AI in clinical decision making. It passed the House 144-59 on September 30, 2026.

bills.title: Providing for consumer protection and for artificial intelligence and chatbots; imposing duties on the Bureau of Consumer Protection in the Office of…
bills.desc: Pennsylvania's HB 2175 (Printer's No. 2831) would add Chapter 71 to Title 12 on AI chatbots that use generative AI to converse with consumers and are represented as helping manage a situation or treat a condition, including mental health. Suppliers could not sell or share health information or consumer input except as allowed, could not advertise in chatbot conversations, and would have to adopt, file and follow a written disclosure policy. Fines up to $2,500 per violation. Introduced January 30, 2026; re-referred to Consumer Protection, Technology & Utilities March 19, 2026; not passed.

bills.title: Providing for artificial intelligence in facilities, for artificial intelligence use by insurers and for artificial intelligence use by MA or CHIP ma…
bills.desc: Pennsylvania's SB 1113 (2025-26) would add rules for AI in health care facilities, AI use by insurers and AI use by MA or CHIP managed care plans, with duties for the departments of Health, Insurance and Human Services and penalties. The captured text covers the facilities chapter: patient disclosure, responsible-use rules and annual AI compliance statements filed with the Department of Health. It was referred to the Senate Institutional Sustainability & Innovation Committee on January 9, 2026.

bills.title: Promotes transparency and accountability in the use of artificial intelligence by health insurers to manage coverage and claims.
bills.desc: Rhode Island H 7190 (2026), as introduced on January 21, 2026, would add chapter 27-84 requiring health insurers to disclose to OHIC and DBR how they use AI to manage claims and coverage and to keep records of AI decisions for at least five years. A non-administrative adverse benefit determination on medically necessary care in which AI made, or was a substantial factor in, the decision would need review and approval by a provider with the same license status as the ordering provider. The text says it takes effect upon passage.
Companion Act to S2197; Oversight of AI in Mental Health Care Act.

bills.title: Requires healthcare providers and healthcare facilities to inform patients of the use of artificial intelligence to memorialize patient visits.
bills.desc: Rhode Island's H 7538 Sub A adds Chapter 23-106 to the General Laws. Healthcare providers and healthcare facilities that use AI to document in-person or telehealth visits must notify patients of the use of AI for that sole purpose and review the AI-generated documentation for accuracy after the visit. The Senate passed Sub A and the House concurred June 11, 2026; signed June 22, 2026 (Chapter 199); effective upon passage (June 22, 2026).

bills.title: Provides that health insurance plans would provide coverage the use of artificial intelligence technology for analysis of breast tissue diagnostic imaging.
bills.desc: Rhode Island H 8073 (2024), as introduced on March 15, 2024, would require individual and group health insurance contracts and plans delivered, issued or renewed in Rhode Island on or after January 1, 2025 to cover the use of AI technology for analysis of breast tissue diagnostic imaging, provided a physician qualified to read such imaging independently reviews and approves the imaging and the AI review. The same text is added in four insurance chapters. The text says it takes effect upon passage.
Oversight of AI in Mental Health Care Act; bars offering therapy via AI unless licensed provider; no independent AI therapeutic decisions.

bills.title: Requires healthcare providers and healthcare facilities to inform patients of the use of artificial intelligence to memorialize patient visits.
bills.desc: Rhode Island S 2570 Substitute A (2026), enacted as Chapter 372, the Use of Artificial Intelligence by Healthcare Providers Notification Act, requires healthcare providers and facilities that use AI to document in-person or telehealth visits to notify patients of the use of AI for that sole purpose and to review the AI-generated documentation for accuracy after the visit. The act states no penalties. Enacted June 22, 2026; effective upon passage.

bills.title: AN ACT RELATING TO INSURANCE -- THE TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE USE BY HEALTH INSURERS TO MANAGE COVERAGE AND CLAIMS ACT
bills.desc: Rhode Island's proposed Transparency and Accountability in AI Use by Health Insurers to Manage Coverage and Claims Act. Health insurers, and contractors acting for them, would have to disclose to the health insurance commissioner and DBR how they use AI in claims and coverage decisions (models, role, training data, performance metrics, governance) and keep records of AI-driven decisions for five years. Any clinical denial in which AI was a substantial factor would need review and approval by a provider with the same license as the ordering provider, or it would be invalid. Regulators would report yearly. The Senate passed a substitute on June 9, 2026.

bills.title: Health Claims & AI
bills.desc: South Carolina's S 443 would add Section 38-59-23 on health care coverage decisions made with artificial intelligence. Actions on coverage decisions could not be based solely on AI results or an automated decision-making tool, and a health care professional would have to supervise and meaningfully review decisions that modify or deny provider authorization requests. Introduced March 11, 2025 and referred to the Senate Banking and Insurance Committee; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: Health insurance
bills.desc: Not law. S. 920 would have required South Carolina health insurers that use AI, algorithms or other software for prior authorization to base decisions on the patient's own medical history and clinical circumstances, have a licensed physician or other qualified professional make every denial, reduction or deferral, tell enrollees that AI is used, certify yearly that their tools are fair and non-discriminatory, and share denial rates on request, with Department of Insurance enforcement. The Senate Banking and Insurance Committee reported it favorably on April 30, 2026, but it was never taken up before the regular session ended.

bills.title: Place requirements on the use of artificial intelligence systems by health carriers in making determinations about the provision of health care services.
bills.desc: South Dakota's SB 169 (2026) would have required health carriers that use AI, algorithms or other software for utilization review to base determinations on the patient's clinical history and circumstances, not rely solely on a group dataset, and apply the tool consistently. AI tools could not deny, delay or modify a determination; only a licensed physician or qualified licensed health professional could make adverse determinations. Introduced January 29, 2026 and withdrawn by the prime sponsor February 17, 2026; it did not pass.

bills.title: AN ACT to amend Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 8, Chapter 27; Title 56 and Title 71, relative to health insurance.
bills.desc: Tennessee's HB 1382 (114th General Assembly) would have required a health insurance issuer that uses AI, an algorithm or other software tool for utilization review or management based on medical necessity to ensure the tool bases decisions on the enrollee's clinical history and circumstances, does not rely solely on a group dataset, does not supplant provider decision-making, and does not discriminate or cause harm. Companion: SB 1261. Not passed before the session ended in April 2026; last action: Assigned to s/c Insurance Subcommittee (February 12, 2025).

bills.title: AN ACT to amend Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 8, Chapter 27; Title 56 and Title 71, relative to health insurance.
bills.desc: Tennessee's HB1866 (114th General Assembly), the "Regulate Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Health Care Act," would have barred, on or after July 1, 2026, a health insurance issuer that uses AI, an algorithm or other software tool for utilization review or management based in whole or in part on medical necessity from denying, delaying or modifying care on medical necessity grounds unless a licensed healthcare professional or provider reviews the prior authorization request. Companion: SB 2010. Not passed before the session ended in April 2026; last action: Taken off notice for cal in s/c Insurance Subcommittee of Insurance Committee (March 11, 2026).

bills.title: AN ACT to amend Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 8, Chapter 27; Title 56 and Title 71, relative to health insurance.
bills.desc: Not law. SB 1261 would have regulated how Tennessee health insurers, TennCare and state employee plans use AI, algorithms and software in utilization review. Tools would have had to base decisions on the patient's own clinical history rather than group data alone, not replace provider judgment or discriminate, and be reviewed periodically. AI could not deny, delay or modify care based on medical necessity; only a licensed physician or qualified health professional could decide that. Violations would have been unfair claims practices, with a right to sue. It never left committee and died when the 114th General Assembly adjourned.
Prohibits deploying an AI system that represents it can act as a qualified mental health professional.

bills.title: Insurance, Health, Accident - As introduced, creates the "Regulate Artificial Intelligence (AI) In Health Care Act." - Amends TCA Title 8, Chapter 27…
bills.desc: Tennessee's SB 2010 (114th General Assembly), the "Regulate Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Health Care Act," would have barred, on or after July 1, 2026, a health insurance issuer that uses AI, an algorithm or other software tool for utilization review or management based in whole or in part on medical necessity from denying, delaying or modifying care on medical necessity grounds unless a licensed healthcare professional or provider reviews the prior authorization request. Companion: HB 1866. Not passed before the session ended in April 2026; last action: Assigned to General Subcommittee of Senate Commerce and Labor Committee (April 7, 2026).

bills.title: Relating to regulation of the use of artificial intelligence systems in this state; providing civil penalties.
bills.desc: Texas's HB 149, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, bars developing or deploying AI intended to incite self-harm, harm to others or crime, with intent to unlawfully discriminate against a protected class (disparate impact alone is not enough), or solely to infringe U.S. constitutional rights, and making or distributing AI solely to produce or spread child pornography or unlawful sexual deep fakes. Government entities may not use AI for harmful social scoring or rights-infringing biometric ID. Agencies must tell consumers they are dealing with AI; health care providers must tell patients. AG enforcement; 60-day cure. Signed June 22, 2025; effective January 1, 2026.

bills.title: Relating to use of artificial intelligence in utilization review conducted for health benefit plans.
bills.desc: Texas HB 2922 (2025), as introduced, would have barred a utilization review agent from using an artificial intelligence-based algorithm as the sole basis for a decision to wholly or partly deny, delay, or modify health care services for an enrollee on medical necessity grounds. Only a physician or licensed health care provider could determine medical necessity, and the insurance commissioner could audit and inspect the agent's use of AI at any time. It did not pass both chambers and died when the session adjourned June 2, 2025.

bills.title: Relating to use of artificial intelligence in utilization review conducted for health benefit plans.
bills.desc: Texas HB 4018 (2025), as introduced, would have added Insurance Code Sec. 4201.156, requiring a utilization review agent that uses an AI-based algorithm or other software tool to ensure it bases determinations on the enrollee's clinical history and circumstances, does not override a physician or provider, and does not discriminate. The agent could not use AI as the sole basis to deny, delay or modify health care services. It died when the regular session adjourned June 2, 2025.

bills.title: Relating to the use of artificial intelligence by health care providers.
bills.desc: Texas HB 4455 (2025), as introduced, would have directed the Health and Human Services executive commissioner to adopt rules regulating health care providers' use of artificial intelligence. The rules would have required a provider using AI to use an automated messaging system when messaging patients that discloses AI use and gives contact information for a provider who can answer questions. It did not pass both chambers and died when the session adjourned June 2, 2025.

bills.title: Relating to electronic health record requirements; authorizing a civil penalty.
bills.desc: Texas's SB 1188 is an electronic health record (EHR) law. Health care practitioners may use AI for diagnostic purposes, including recommendations on a diagnosis or course of treatment based on a patient's medical record, if acting within their license, the use is not otherwise restricted by law, and they review all AI-created records consistent with Texas Medical Board standards; they must disclose that use to patients. EHRs must be kept physically in the U.S. or a U.S. territory (for storage from January 1, 2026), and EHR algorithms that aid treatment decisions must include the recorded biological sex. AG civil penalties apply. Signed June 20, 2025; effective September 1, 2025.

bills.title: Relating to the use of artificial intelligence-based algorithms by health benefit plan issuers, utilization review agents, health care providers, and…
bills.desc: Texas SB 1411 (2025), as introduced, would have regulated AI-based algorithms in health coverage and care. Health benefit plan issuers and physicians could not discriminate on race, color, national origin, gender, age, vaccination status or disability using clinical AI algorithms. Issuers would have had to disclose AI use in utilization review, submit algorithms and training data to the insurance department, and have a specialist review before an adverse determination. Physicians and providers could have faced license sanctions and fines up to $5,000 per violation. It died June 2, 2025.

bills.title: Relating to the use of artificial intelligence-based algorithms in utilization review conducted for certain health benefit plans.
bills.desc: Texas SB 1822 (2025), as engrossed, would have added Insurance Code Sec. 4201.156 requiring health benefit plan issuers and their utilization review agents to disclose whether they use AI-based algorithms in utilization review, ensure the algorithm and its training data minimize bias and follow evidence-based clinical guidelines, and file an annual compliance statement by December 31. It passed the Senate, but no enrolled version exists, so it died June 2, 2025.

A utilization review agent may not use an automated decision system to make an adverse determination, wholly or partly; only a physician or licensed provider may determine medical necessity. The Department of Insurance may audit AI use.

bills.title: HEAL-AI Act Healthcare Education in AI Literacy Act
bills.desc: The federal H.R. 6077 (HEAL-AI Act, Healthcare Education in AI Literacy Act) would amend the Public Health Service Act to create a Health Resources and Services Administration competitive grant program, with grants of up to $100,000 a year, for medical schools and residency sponsors to train students, residents and faculty in using AI in medicine. Referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee November 18, 2025; it has not passed either chamber.

bills.title: AI in Health Care Efficiency and Study Act
bills.desc: The federal H.R. 7064 (AI in Health Care Efficiency and Study Act) would require the Secretary of Health and Human Services, not later than 18 months after enactment, to conduct a study of strategies for applying AI across the health care industry to improve administrative and clerical processes while protecting patient data privacy and security in HHS programs and activities. The Secretary would report to Congress 6 months after finishing the study. Introduced January 14, 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee; no further action.

bills.title: Right to Override Act
bills.desc: The federal S. 2997 (Right to Override Act) would require covered entities that employ or engage health care professionals and use AI clinical decision support (AI/CDSS) to adopt an override policy, train staff and run an AI/CDSS committee, and would bar adverse employment action or retaliation for overriding an AI output. HHS would enforce Title I with civil monetary penalties; Labor would enforce Title II with penalties up to $76,987 per violation ($769,870 for repeats), alongside a private right of action. Introduced October 9, 2025 and referred to the Senate HELP Committee; no further action.

bills.title: Artificial Intelligence Amendments
bills.desc: Utah's HB 452 regulates mental health chatbots: generative AI that holds therapy-like conversations and that the supplier represents, or a reasonable person would believe, can provide mental health therapy or help manage mental health conditions. Suppliers may not sell or share Utah users' identifiable health information or input (limited exceptions), may not use input to target or tailor ads, must label in-chat ads, and must disclose the chatbot is AI before access, after seven days of non-use and when asked. Fines up to $2,500 per violation. Signed March 25, 2025; effective May 7, 2025.
Scope-of-practice limit; AI that solely advises/treats without practitioner-patient interaction is not a qualifying technology innovation.
Insurers must disclose AI use in preauthorization; adverse determination reviewer must use independent medical judgment.

bills.title: An act relating to the use of artificial intelligence in health care coverage decisions
bills.desc: Vermont's H.776 (2026) would have added 18 V.S.A. 9423 on AI in health care coverage decisions. A health plan using an AI tool, algorithm or software for utilization review would have had to base determinations on the insured's clinical history and circumstances, not rely solely on a group dataset, apply it consistently, allow Department of Financial Regulation audits, and review it at least quarterly. AI could not deny, delay or modify coverage; adverse determinations would have been made only by a licensed human provider. Referred to committee January 27, 2026; died.

bills.title: An act relating to neurological rights and the use of artificial intelligence technology in health and human services
bills.desc: Act 101 states Vermont's intent for the ethical and responsible use of AI in health care and human services and recognizes individual neurological rights, including mental and neural data privacy, freedom of thought, and protection from unauthorized access to or manipulation of brain activity (18 V.S.A. ch. 42C). It adds members to the state Artificial Intelligence Advisory Council, extends the Council to June 30, 2030, and directs it to report by January 15, 2027 on neurological-rights protections, generative AI use by regulated professions, and AI in health insurance utilization review. Effective May 18, 2026.
Therapy chatbot ban; mental health services must be delivered by professionals not independently by AI.
AI may not be the sole means to deny, delay or modify health care services; medical-necessity denials require review by a licensed provider. Two sections take effect January 1, 2027.
